meta.title: BoxBox · Who wins on Sunday?
meta.description: Win and podium chances for the next F1 race from the starting grid, the circuit and the race-day forecast. An XGBoost model trained on real results since 2018 and refit after every Grand Prix.

how.title: How the model works
how.lede: An end-to-end guide for people who write code every day and know machine learning in theory, but haven't shipped it: where the data comes from, how it becomes features, what XGBoost does inside, how to validate without cheating, and what the metrics actually mean.
how.readingTime: About a 15-minute read · Every number on this page comes from the deployed model, not from hand-written copy.

short.title: The short version
body: BoxBox solves a **supervised classification** problem. Each example is **one driver in one race**, and the model answers: what's the chance this driver wins, finishes 2nd or 3rd, or misses the podium?

Think of it as a pure function `f(features) → [p_win, p_podium, p_rest]` whose parameters nobody writes by hand: they are **fitted** by looking at {rows} real examples (from {from} to {to}, {races} races). That's all training is: finding the parameters that make the function as right as possible on data we already know, hoping it stays right on data it hasn't seen.

That last sentence is the whole craft. A model that's only right on its training data is useless. Almost everything below (how features are built, how it's validated, why the model is small) exists so the model **generalises** to races it hasn't seen.

pipeline.title: The pipeline, end to end
body: If you come from software, an ML system looks more like a **build** than a feature: an offline phase produces an artefact (the trained model) and an online phase loads it and serves requests. Every step lives in the monorepo: `boxbox-ml/` (data and training), `backend/` (API) and `frontend/` (this site).

steps.name: Extract
steps.detail: Race results and qualifying for every GP from Jolpica (the Ergast API's successor), and the weather for the first two hours of the race from Open-Meteo. Stored as Parquet, one row per driver per race.

steps.name: Features
steps.detail: Turns raw data into the columns the model understands: grid slot, recent form, how hard the track is to pass on… Using only what's known before lights out.

steps.name: Train and validate
steps.detail: A race-by-race backtest to measure how well it predicts, then a final fit on all the data. Produces `model.joblib` (≈300 KB) and `metrics.json`.

steps.name: Serve
steps.detail: Loads the model once at startup. Exposes the calendar with forecasts, predictions and the track record. Runs on Render.

steps.name: Show
steps.detail: Calls the API from the server (never from the browser) and draws the pit board, the table and this guide. Runs on Vercel.

data.title: The data
body: One row of the dataset is **one driver in one Grand Prix**: starting slot, qualifying position, gap to pole in %, team, circuit, weather and how they finished. That's {rows} rows from {races} races.

We use every season since 2018. We first tried 2022 onwards, when the technical rules changed (ground-effect cars), because in ML **more data isn't always better**: data from a different world than the one you're predicting can teach things that are no longer true (*distribution shift*). Instead of assuming it, we measured it with the same race-by-race validation: adding 2018-2021 lowered log loss from 0.2915 to 0.2788 and raised the favourite's hit rate from 53 % to 62 %. With so few winners, the extra years mattered more than the rule change, so they stayed.

Historical weather comes from ERA5 reanalysis, an hour-by-hour reconstruction of the atmosphere, averaged over the two hours from the start. Upcoming races use the forecast, with the same aggregation code. More than 1 mm of rain in that window makes the race count as wet. The threshold was chosen from real cases: Suzuka 2025 was dry and ERA5 showed 0.5 mm.

What we **don't** have: telemetry, lap times, tyre strategy or pit stops. FastF1 offers them, but it needs a paid F1 TV subscription. It's a real limit of the model, and worth keeping in mind when you read its predictions.

target.title: What exactly we predict
body: The **target** (or *label*) is what the model learns to predict. We could predict the exact position (1, 2, 3… 22), but that's very noisy: finishing 14th or 15th comes down to near-random things we don't care about. So the outcome is grouped into three classes:
after: For each driver the model returns three probabilities that add up to 1. The podium chance is simply `p(win) + p(2nd–3rd)`, so **it can never be lower than the win chance**. Two separate models (one for wins, one for podiums) could contradict each other.

Notice the **imbalance**: winning is rare, about 4–5 % of rows. A dumb model that said “nobody ever wins” would be 95 % accurate and completely useless. That's why accuracy isn't our main metric; more on that in the metrics section.

features.title: Features: where it's won or lost
body: A **feature** is a numeric column the model can use to decide. The algorithm only sees numbers: it doesn't know what a driver is or what Monaco is. Feature engineering means translating domain knowledge into useful columns. With little data, as here, it usually matters more than the choice of algorithm.
These are the model's {count} features, grouped by the question they answer:

items.label: Grid slot
items.what: By far the strongest feature. Pit-lane starters are placed behind the last car.

items.label: Qualifying position
items.what: Usually equal to the grid slot unless there are penalties. When they differ, it gives away a quick car starting further back.

items.label: Gap to pole (%)
items.what: How much slower they were in qualifying, as a percentage. Tells a 0.05 % pole from a 0.5 % one.

items.label: Temperature
items.what: Air temperature over the first two hours of the race.

items.label: Humidity
items.what: Average relative humidity.

items.label: Wind
items.what: Average wind speed in m/s.

items.label: Rain
items.what: 1 if at least 1 mm fell (or is forecast) in that window. Rain shuffles the grid order.

items.label: Circuit
items.what: A categorical feature: XGBoost learns each track's quirks without us hand-coding them.

items.label: How hard to pass
items.what: The correlation between start order and finish order at that circuit's previous editions. Close to 1 means you finish where you start (Monaco); lower means comebacks happen.

items.label: Grid × difficulty
items.what: The product of the two above. It hands the model the idea, ready-made, that starting 8th means something different at Monaco than at Monza.

items.label: Average finish (last 5)
items.what: Recent form: where they finished on average in their 5 previous races.

items.label: Average points (last 5)
items.what: Like the one above, but it rewards top results more.

items.label: Places gained (last 5)
items.what: How many places they usually make up in the race. Some drivers and cars are better on Sunday than on Saturday.

items.label: Retirement rate (last 10)
items.what: Recent reliability of driver and car.

items.label: Experience
items.what: Races in the dataset so far.

items.label: Track history
items.what: Their average finish at previous editions of the same GP.

items.label: Wet-race history
items.what: Their average finish in races with rain.

items.label: Team points (last 5)
items.what: Points from both cars combined. It's our best stand-in for how fast the car is right now.

features.tried: We also tried features that **didn't** make it: car pace in qualifying, whole-season form and grid penalties. They didn't improve the backtest, so they were removed. Features that add nothing just give the model more ways to be wrong.
features.leakTitle: The golden rule: nothing from the future
leak: The most common (and most expensive) mistake in ML is **data leakage**: the model sees, during training, information it wouldn't have at the real moment of prediction. Tests look spectacular, then it collapses in production.

A concrete example: if a driver's “recent form” included the result of the very race we're predicting, the model would learn to copy it. It would ace the tests, and in a real race that number wouldn't exist yet.
That's why every form feature is computed **after shifting one row**: for each race only earlier races count. In pandas it's a `shift(1)` within each driver:
features.code:
# Recent form: mean of each driver's 5 PREVIOUS races
previous = df.groupby("driver_ref")["finish"].shift(1)  # drop the current race
form = previous.groupby(df["driver_ref"]).rolling(5, min_periods=1).mean()
features.skewTitle: Same code to train and to predict
skew: The second classic mistake is *training-serving skew*: a feature is computed one way during training and a slightly different way in the API. It's like validating a form with different rules on the client and on the server.

Here's how we avoid it: when you ask for a prediction, the API appends your hypothetical race as one more row at the end of the history and runs **exactly the same** `build_features` function used for training. There's no second implementation to drift out of sync.

model.title: The algorithm: XGBoost
body: The model is a **gradient-boosted ensemble of decision trees** (the XGBoost library). It's the go-to for tabular data, meaning rows and columns like a spreadsheet. On problems like this it usually beats neural networks, especially with little data.

**A decision tree** is a stack of `if/else` statements learned from data. The algorithm tries splits like “grid ≤ 2?” or “rain = 1?” and keeps the ones that best separate winners from everyone else. One tree on its own is readable but clumsy.
model.treeCaption: A small, illustrative tree (real ones ask up to 4 questions deep)
boosting: **Boosting** means training trees **in sequence**, each one small and focused on fixing the errors left by the ones before. It's a bit like refactoring in iterations: the first tree catches the big picture (starting up front helps), the next one looks at the cases the first got wrong (the driver who started 6th and won in the rain), and so on. The final prediction is the **sum** of every tree, turned into three probabilities with a *softmax*.
The deployed model has {trees} trees. We didn't pick that number by hand: *early stopping* chose it, as explained below.
model.paramsIntro: **Parameters** are what the model learns (each tree's splits). **Hyperparameters** are what we set before training: the algorithm's configuration. Nearly all of them serve one purpose, keeping the model from memorising:

params.name: max_depth
params.what: Each tree asks at most 4 questions in a row. Shallow trees capture general patterns, not one-off cases.

params.name: learning_rate
params.what: Each new tree only corrects 3 % of what it could. Small steps need more trees but give a steadier result.

params.name: min_child_weight
params.what: No branch is created for a handful of examples. It prevents rules like “if it's Monaco 2023 and raining, X wins”.

params.name: subsample · colsample_bytree
params.what: Each tree sees a random 80 % of the rows and 80 % of the columns. That noise forces it not to lean on any single data point.

params.name: reg_lambda
params.what: Penalises trees that make large jumps. This is regularisation: putting a price on complexity.

params.name: n_estimators
params.what: The tree cap. Early stopping sets the real number.

overfit: **Overfitting** happens when the model memorises the noise in its training data instead of the pattern. It's like a test suite that only passes with the exact fixtures you wrote it against: green in CI, red in production.
With about 2,000 rows the risk is high, so the model is deliberately small and conservative.
model.dropoutTitle: A practical trick: hiding data on purpose
model.dropout: The API accepts predictions with only the grid slot, without the gap to pole. If the model had always seen that gap during training, it wouldn't know what to do when it's missing. So during training it's **erased at random in 30 % of rows**. It's a kind of *chaos testing*: the model learns to work even when that data is missing.

validation.title: Validating without cheating
body: To know whether a model works you have to test it on data it **didn't** see during training. The textbook recipe is to shuffle the rows and hold out a random 20 %. Here that would be a serious mistake: the model would train on 2026 races to “predict” 2024 ones. That's peeking at the future, and the future (which car is quick this year) is exactly what we're trying to predict.
When data depends on time, validation has to respect the order. We use a **race-by-race walk-forward backtest**, which mirrors exactly how the model would be used in real life:
steps: Before every GP of the last three seasons, a new model is trained **only on earlier races**.
That model predicts the GP's whole field.
The prediction is saved and compared with the real result.
The result joins the training data and we move on to the next race.
after: That's {backtestRaces} full training runs (about 4 minutes on a laptop). Every prediction in the **Track record** comes from here: it's what the model would really have said before that race.

**Early stopping**: inside each training run we hold out the most recent 15 % of races and keep adding trees while the error on those races goes down. After 100 trees with no improvement we stop and keep the best count. Then the model is refit on everything with that count. That's where the {trees}-tree figure comes from.
The deployed model is trained on **every** race, including the latest. That's why it has to be retrained after each GP: that's how it learns from what just happened.
validation.timelineCaption: Walk-forward: each race is predicted by a model that only knows the past

metrics.title: How we measure it
body: There's no single metric: each one answers a different question. These come from the backtest ({backtestRaces} races), compared with a **baseline**.
metrics.baselineTitle: The baseline: always compare with the simple thing
metrics.baseline: The baseline is a logistic regression that **only looks at the grid slot**. It basically says “whoever starts ahead has better odds”. It's the equivalent of benchmarking your optimised algorithm against the naive implementation: if it doesn't win, the complexity isn't worth it. In ML it's surprisingly common for a sophisticated model to fail to beat the obvious rule.

items.name: Log loss
items.what: Checks whether the **probabilities** are good, not just the order. It punishes being confidently wrong very hard. Say 95 % and the driver doesn't win: huge penalty. Say 30 % and they don't win: barely anything. It's the metric training optimises.

items.name: Win AUC
items.what: Pick one driver who won and one who didn't at random: how often did the model rate the winner higher? It measures how well the whole field is ordered.

items.name: Favourite wins
items.what: In what share of races the driver the model rated highest actually won. The most intuitive metric and the noisiest: it hangs on one row per race.

items.name: Top 3 on the podium
items.what: Of the model's three most likely podium finishers, how many made the podium on average.

reading: **How to read it**: the model wins on log loss and AUC. It orders the whole field better and its probabilities are better calibrated. But when it must name a single winner, it's right less often than “pole sitter wins”.

That isn't a contradiction. In this era pole turns into victory very often, and the simple rule always backs the same candidate. The model spreads probability across several candidates, and when its favourite isn't the pole sitter it often falls short. To back a single name, the simple rule is hard to beat. To know **how much** more likely one driver is than another, the model is better. That's why the site shows probabilities, not a winner.

normalize.title: From loose probabilities to a coherent board
body: The model scores each driver **independently**: to it, every row stands alone. So if you add up all 22 drivers' win chances you don't get exactly 100 %. It might be 93 % or 108 %, which makes no sense in a race with one winner.

The API fixes that after predicting: it rescales the win chances to add up to 100 % and the podium chances to add up to 300 % (there are three places). It respects two rules: no podium chance can go above 100 %, and none can be lower than the win chance. If a driver would go over 100 %, they're held at the cap and the rest is shared among the others (known as *water-filling*).
It's a small step, but it shows something important: a model's raw output is almost never what you show the user. There's always a layer of product logic on top.

importance.title: Which features matter most
body: XGBoost keeps track of how much the prediction improved each time it used a feature to split a tree. This is called **gain**. Shared out as percentages, it hints at what the deployed model pays attention to:
importance.caveat: Two warnings. Importance **is not causation**: grid slot weighing so much doesn't prove that starting up front “causes” the win, because the fast car starts up front **and** wins. And when two features say almost the same thing (grid and qualifying), they split the importance between them fairly arbitrarily.

serving.title: In production
body: The trained model is a `model.joblib` file of about 300 KB, versioned in the repository. It holds the trees, the list of known circuits and the results history needed to compute recent form. The API (FastAPI, on Render) loads it **once** at startup, and from then on each prediction takes milliseconds.

The calendar comes from Jolpica and each race's forecast from Open-Meteo. Both are kept in memory for an hour, so the site doesn't depend on those services answering on every visit. The forecast only arrives once the race is 14 days away or less; before that, the model works without weather and assumes a dry track.

Every prediction requested is logged in Postgres (Neon) with the model version. Later on, that makes it possible to measure whether the model gets worse over time (*model drift*), which in F1 happens as soon as a team brings car upgrades.

retrain.title: Automatic retraining after every GP
body: An F1 model goes stale fast. The form features (points over the last 5 races, average finish, retirements…) are only current if the model knows the latest race, and every weekend brings something new: a car that improves, a driver losing pace. Without retraining, the model keeps predicting with the world of weeks ago.

So retraining is automated with **GitHub Actions**, the repository's own CI, in `.github/workflows/retrain.yml`. It's exactly what you'd do by hand, but run by a machine, with checks that stop a worse model from shipping.
retrain.trigger: It runs **every day at 06:00 UTC** (and can be started by hand). Jolpica publishes results a few hours after the chequered flag, so they're there the morning after a GP. On other days the job sees nothing new and finishes in about a minute. The design is **idempotent**: running it twice changes nothing, so it doesn't need to know when each race is, or worry about Saturday races or calendar changes.
retrain.stepsTitle: What it does, step by step
steps: **Downloads** the current season's results and weather. Finished seasons and HTTP responses are cached between runs, so only new data is requested again.
**Compares** the latest race with results against the last one the deployed model knows (`data_to` in `metrics.json`). If they match, it stops here.

**Trains** exactly as it does locally: the race-by-race backtest over the last three seasons (which now includes the GP that just ended as one more Track-record prediction) and the final fit on all the data.
**Quality gate**: the new model must still beat the grid-only baseline on log loss and AUC. If it doesn't, the job fails on purpose, the deployed model stays untouched and GitHub sends an email.
**API tests** against the new model: the same ones run in development, so a file the API can't load, or one that returns nonsense probabilities, never ships.
**Loads the new results into Neon** (drivers, circuits and entries), if the repository has the database connection secret configured.

**Commits and pushes** `model.joblib` and `metrics.json`. That push is the deploy: Render rebuilds the API with the new model and Vercel rebuilds the site. Within minutes the pit board, the Track record and the numbers in this guide reflect the race that just happened.
why: **The model lives in git.** Each retrain is a commit with the model and its metrics. Rolling back is a `git revert`, and the repository history doubles as the model's version history. Large teams use a *model registry* for this; with a 300 KB file, git is enough.

**A quality gate, not faith.** Just as you don't merge code with red tests, a model that can't beat the obvious rule doesn't ship. It's the minimum version of what MLOps calls *continuous training* with automatic validation.

**What it doesn't do yet**: it doesn't watch for drift between races or alert when predictions start missing more than usual. The data for that is already logged in the predictions table; it's the natural next step.

limits.title: Honest limits
items: **Little data.** About 2,000 rows and only around a hundred winners. Each rare win (a driver winning from 9th in the rain) weighs a lot, and it's hard to tell pattern from noise.
**Half the sport is missing.** Without telemetry, race pace, strategy, tyres or safety cars, the model can't see many of the things that decide a race.
**The world changes.** The 2026 rules changed the cars, and team form shifts with every upgrade. Weighting recent races more, or detecting these changes automatically, is a natural next step.
**You set the grid.** Before qualifying, the model uses the last race's starting order as a guess. Its quality depends on that grid looking like the real one.

**Probabilities are probabilities.** 40 % means that, in similar situations, that driver wins about 4 times in 10. Losing today doesn't prove the model wrong, and winning doesn't prove it right either. To judge it you have to look at many races: that's what the Track record is for.

terms.def: An input column the model uses to decide.
What you want to predict; here, win, podium or rest.
Fitting the model's parameters so it's right on data we already know.
Algorithm configuration set before training (tree depth, learning rate…).
Memorising training noise: good in tests, bad on new data.
Information that wouldn't exist at prediction time sneaking into training.
Validation that respects time: predict each moment using only the past.
A simple solution to compare against; if you can't beat it, the model isn't worth it.
When the model says 30 %, it really happens about 30 % of the time.
Stop adding trees once the error on held-out data stops falling.

history.title: How good is it?
history.lede: Before every Grand Prix of the last three seasons the model was trained only on the earlier races and predicted the whole grid. Here is each prediction next to what actually happened.
history.caption: Predicted order by win chance (normalised over the grid), with the real finishing position on the right.
history.winnerRankHint: Where the eventual winner sat in our list on average (1 = our favourite).
history.allHint: Tap a race to see its full prediction.

why.title: Why {driver}?
why.intro: Their win chance is {p}. These are the inputs that moved it most, computed with SHAP: how much each input adds to the model's output. Tap another driver in the table to see theirs.
why.none: No input stands out: the prediction sits close to the average.
why.note: Each factor multiplies the odds of winning: ×2 doubles them, ×0.5 halves them. Minor factors are left out.

championship.title: Who wins the title?
championship.lede: We simulate the {races} races left of the {season} season {sims} times and count how often each driver ends up champion.
championship.none: The season is over: no races left to simulate.
championship.methodBody: Each remaining race is a sequential draw (Plackett-Luce): the model gives every driver a weight from their chance to win the next race and the draw hands out the 25-to-1 points. It leaves out sprints and retirements and uses the same strength at every circuit: a guide, not a forecast.
championship.unavailable: We could not read the calendar. Try again in a few minutes.
championship.sub: Each driver's title odds, from the model and the current points.

drivers.title: Drivers
drivers.lede: The current grid. Open a driver to see recent form and what the model expected from them.
drivers.modelHint: Win chance the model gave them before the race (only for audited races).
drivers.notFound: That driver is not in the data.
drivers.unavailable: We could not load the profile. Try again in a few minutes.

quality.calibrationLede: When the model says 30 %, does it happen 30 % of the time? Each pair of bars groups predictions of similar probability: the light bar is what was predicted, the dark one what happened.
quality.applied: Corrected with calibration: squared error over the last {n} races went from {raw} to {cal}.
quality.notApplied: Left uncorrected: over the last {n} races it did not lower the error ({raw} vs {cal}).
quality.calibrationNote: The probabilities on this page are the uncorrected model's; live predictions already carry the correction when it is applied.
quality.driftLede: Error of every audited race (lower is better). Last {window}: {recent}; whole record: {overall}. It flags when the recent ones run 25 % above the average.
quality.liveLede: The predictions people made on the site before each race, compared with what happened.
quality.liveEmpty: No races with logged predictions and a result yet.
quality.liveOff: The prediction log is not available right now.
